answer:
ANSWER: The variable is RACE — specifically the Black category relative to the White reference group (SAMPLE_RACE).

Rationale (data-grounded): In the full model BA ~ RACE + SES + ABILITY + PERC, the Black(White-ref) logistic coefficient is +0.0926 (≈ the target 0.0923, diff 0.0003) and is statistically INsignificant (p=0.68). No other candidate lands on 0.0923 or loses significance:
  • FAMILY SIZE does NOT shrink — it stays −0.5085, p<0.0001 (still highly significant) in the full model.
  • SEX (Female) was already insignificant (univariate p=0.125) and moves to 0.2235, p=0.113 — it does not drop to 0.0923.
  • Only the RACE (Black) coefficient both lands on ~0.0923 and crosses from significant to insignificant.

The mechanism: the Black–White gap in BA completion is large and significant in the baseline (univariate Black coef = −1.0057, p<0.0001) but essentially vanishes once SES and academic characteristics (ASVAB ability + class percentile) are controlled — i.e., the racial difference in degree completion is largely mediated by / explained through socioeconomic background and academic preparation, not an independent effect of race.

Honest caveat on the exact 0.5024 (flagged, not force-fitted): the pure-univariate baseline gives −1.0057, not +0.5024. The full-model 0.0923 side reproduces essentially exactly; the 0.5024 "before" value does not reproduce from the pure-univariate spec, so the source study's baseline likely used a slightly different specification/subsample (nearest control-inclusive baseline I found: RACE+SEX+FS+ABILITY+PERC = 0.4888). The shrinkage-and-loss-of-significance pattern uniquely identifies RACE regardless, so the identification is robust.

One-paragraph natural-language hypothesis (final answer):
"The effect of RACE on BA degree completion — specifically being Black versus the White reference group — decreases from a significant value (~0.50) to 0.0923 and becomes statistically insignificant once both socioeconomic status (SES) and academic characteristics (ASVAB ability composite and in-class percentile) are included. This shows that the Black–White difference in completing a bachelor's degree is largely explained by differences in socioeconomic background and academic preparation; after controlling for SES and academic ability, race no longer has an independent, significant effect on degree completion."

This shows that the Black–White difference in completing a bachelor's degree is largely explained by differences in socioeconomic background and academic preparation; after controlling for SES and academic ability, race no longer has an independent, significant effect on degree completion.
payload.workflow: Loaded nls_ses_processed.csv (N=8773; 236 BA completions, 2.69%; no missing; no perfect separation; all logistic fits converged). (1) Fit univariate logistic models BA~X for every candidate X (race dummies under White/Black/Hispanic references, sex, family size) and recorded coefficient/p. (2) Fit full models BA~X+SES+ABILITY+PERC for each X. (3) Compared: only the RACE Black(White-ref) coefficient lands on 0.0926 (~0.0923) and loses significance (p=0.68); family size stays -0.5085 (sig) and sex stays ~0.22 (ns) — so RACE is the unique match. Ran an exhaustive subset search to locate the 0.5024 baseline spec (not force-fitted; pure-univariate gives -1.0057).
